questions.mappingNote: Question 1 assesses parallel-line angle reasoning and its converse; the generalisation in c follows the same angle relationships used in a.
questions.methodNote: Use the local equal-angle reflection rule, straight-angle sums, alternate angles between parallel mirrors and the converse alternate-angle test.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines reflection, parallel-line angle relationships and a generalisation used to recognise parallel rays.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect equal reflection angles with supplementary and vertically opposite angles across two triangles, then generalise the numerical angle chase to show that y cancels and the elevation is 2x. The supplied diagram, reflection rule and preceding numerical cases scaffold this connection.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 applies the reflection rule twice, then triangle angle sums to calculate and generalise the angle of elevation. The triangle-angle skill is the closest catalogue match to the most advanced directly assessed method.
questions.methodNote: The local reflection rule states that incoming and outgoing rays make equal angles with the mirror. The inspected Chapter 7 evidence teaches supplementary angles, vertically opposite angles and triangle angle sums, with reasons and algebraic working.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect equal reflection angles with supplementary and vertically opposite angles across two triangles, then generalise the numerical angle chase to show that y cancels and the elevation is 2x. classification.difficultyReason: Explicitly staged count, single adjacent-gap Pythagoras and sum of named components lead to the standard formula. Several linked familiar procedures are required, but each geometric component and generalisation is prompted.

questions.mappingNote: Chapter 2 page 2 supplies the unknown-hypotenuse method. Chapter 6 page 15 supplies formula-construction context; page 19 supplies the progression from numerical counts to general counting expressions. None supplies a lacing-specific result.
questions.methodNote: Count two diagonal segments per gap between adjacent eyelet levels. Apply Pythagoras' theorem to perpendicular distances d and g, then construct the total-length formula by adding all segment types.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Generalise a visibly scaffolded count to2(n-1), recognise the right-triangle diagonal and use Pythagoras symbolically, then combine those two earlier results with the bottom gap and two free ends. This links familiar pattern, geometric and algebraic procedures; the explicit staged prompts remove the need for an unsignposted modelling insight.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied component sequence to count horizontal and short-diagonal segments, model the full-height return with Pythagoras and combine terms. The longer symbolic expression adds coordination, while the model decomposition is already specified.

questions.mappingNote: Pythagoras in a practical model is the most advanced directly assessed method; general counting expressions support it.
questions.methodNote: Count repeated segments, express their lengths algebraically, and use Pythagoras' theorem for short and long diagonals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the explicitly staged count-to-formula prompts, recognise short and full-height right triangles, apply Pythagoras in symbols and combine four component lengths. There are several linked familiar procedures and a longer symbolic expression, but the sequence identifies each required component and removes an unsignposted model choice.

classification.difficultyReason: Select useful trials across several parameters, compare two symbolic route models and infer which pattern is shorter including the two-pair equality case. The investigation supplies no test strategy or comparison reduction, so students must organise evidence and generalise beyond routine substitution.

questions.mappingNote: Practical Pythagorean modelling remains the main skill; numerical substitution provides the requested investigation.
questions.methodNote: Use counted segment lengths and Pythagoras to construct the models, then investigate numerical cases. A general algebraic proof is not required by the source task.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose meaningful parameter trials, compare the two preceding general formulas fairly and infer when one pattern is shorter, including the boundary case. This open investigation requires selecting and evaluating a comparison strategy rather than executing a named calculation, while the prior formulas provide substantial support.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the correct square and equilateral-triangle regions between tangent circles, choose sector subtraction and derive a triangle altitude before calculating the gaps. Intermediate side/height prompts scaffold the algebra, but composite-region selection remains an independent geometric decision.

questions.mappingNote: Circle and composite-area geometry support the Packaging task; cross-sectional-area volume applies to Q2. Preserve the complete printed whole question in its own owner.
questions.methodNote: Subtract sectors from half a square and an equilateral triangle. Use the attached Year8 circle-area/sector exercises and original Year9 Pythagoras teaching; no new method is introduced.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret shaded tangent-circle gaps, choose square/sector subtraction and connect an equilateral-triangle altitude to Pythagoras before subtracting sectors. The intermediate side/height questions scaffold the work, but identifying the correct composite regions requires geometric method selection.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct three different tight-wrap cross-sectional decompositions from tangent-circle arrangements, combine triangle/rectangle and sector areas with Pythagoras, extrude by the fixed height and compare. The prompts name only arrangements and desired volumes, so the multi-step geometric models must be selected independently; no general proof or novel theorem is required.

questions.mappingNote: Circle and composite-area geometry support the Packaging task; cross-sectional-area volume applies to Q2. Preserve the complete printed whole question in its own owner.
questions.methodNote: Decompose the tight-wrap planar hull into rectangle/triangle and circular sectors, then use original constant-cross-sectional-area volume V=Ah with h=20cm; compare three computed volumes.
